plan: [ In a sealed-bid second-price auction, the weakly dominant strategy is to bid your true value because your bid only affects whether you win, not the price you pay (which is the second-highest bid). With a value of $6 and no meaningful history in a single round, shading risks losing positive-surplus wins; overbidding risks negative surplus if a rival’s value slightly exceeds yours. Therefore, bid exactly your value to win whenever the second-highest bid is below $6. ]

[ Second-price auctions make truthful bidding optimal. With independent private values drawn uniformly each round and only 1 round, there’s no benefit to strategic shading or signaling. Bidding my value ensures I win exactly when the second-highest bid is below my value and I never pay above it. Tie-breaking is random; bidding exactly my value remains optimal. Therefore, to maximize expected profit this round, I will bid my true value of $40. ]

[ In a sealed-bid second-price auction with independent private values and risk-neutral preferences, the dominant strategy is to bid your true value. Overbidding risks winning when the price exceeds value; underbidding risks losing profitable wins. With one round and no history to exploit, maximizing expected profit means setting the threshold at my valuation. Values are uniform 0–49; my value is $28, so I bid 28 to win whenever the highest competing bid is below 28 and pay that competing bid. ]
